summary:
South Sudan's Penal Code reaches gender presentation on its face: it criminalises "any male person who dresses or is attired in the fashion of a woman", with a penalty of up to three months' imprisonment. For a trans visitor presenting female, that provision is the operative exposure. It requires no sexual conduct and no disclosure of identity.

The same law treats consensual same-sex sexual conduct as "unnatural offenses", defined as carnal intercourse against the order of nature, punishable by up to 10 years' imprisonment. Where the conduct is nonconsensual, the term rises to up to 14 years.

United States State Department country reports on human rights practices for 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2022 each record that there were no reports of authorities enforcing the same-sex conduct provision. Those reports describe no repeal, no moratorium and no prosecutorial policy behind the non-enforcement, so the statute remains in force.

The reported non-enforcement of the conduct provision does not describe the wider picture for a visible trans person. The same State Department reporting across 2018 to 2022 documents security forces routinely harassing LGBTQI+ persons and, in some cases, arresting, detaining, beating and torturing them. In 2017 security forces raided Access for All, a community-based LGBTQ-supportive organisation; its staff were detained for several months and released without charge, and the organisation was intimidated into closing, its executive director later leaving the country.

Official hostility is stated in explicit terms. In September 2017 the minister for Labour, Public Service and Human Resource Development, Gathoth Gatkuoth Hothnyang, said the government would order security forces to arrest LGBTQ persons and detain them until they procreate. No such arrests were reported by the end of that year. The State Department's 2022 report found that most openly LGBTQI+ citizens had fled South Sudan because of actively hostile government rhetoric and action.

Protection machinery for a visitor who is targeted is absent. The country has no anti-discrimination or hate-crime legislation protecting LGBTQ persons from harassment or abuse on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex couples have no legal recognition, and same-sex marriage has been constitutionally banned since the Constitution was adopted in 2011.

Societal conditions raise the likelihood of non-state violence. LGBTQ people face widespread stigmatisation among the broader population, the 2011 State Department report found "widespread" societal discrimination against gay men and lesbians, and the country has no known LGBTQ-support organisations to which a traveller could turn after an incident.
tangentialFactors:
The hostility recorded in government statements predates independence. In July 2010 then-President Salva Kiir Mayardit said homosexuality is not in the "character" of Southern Sudanese people and would never gain support, and in 2006 Bishop Abraham Mayom Athiaan split from the Episcopal Church of Sudan over what he treated as insufficient condemnation of homosexuality.

Detention without charge has been used against people associated with LGBTQ advocacy rather than against individuals for conduct alone. The Access for All staff held after the 2017 raid were released without charge after several months, which indicates an administrative route to coercion that sits alongside the Penal Code provisions.

The reporting that documents non-enforcement of the same-sex conduct provision simultaneously documents beatings, torture and arbitrary detention by security forces, so state practice in this area is not uniform across instruments.
localsOnly:
As of 2020, harassment of employees based on sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited for all oil and gas companies operating in the country. This is the only sectoral exception identified to the general absence of discrimination protection.

The Non-Governmental Organisations Act 2016 bars organisations from contravening the country's sovereignty, its institutions and laws. Because same-sex activity is criminal, that provision constrains LGBTQ-supportive civic groups from organising, and the practical result is that no support organisation currently operates.

Residents face the same Penal Code exposure as visitors and, unlike short-term travellers, no realistic domestic remedy: no hate-crime provision, no anti-discrimination statute outside the oil and gas sector, and documented abuse by security forces between 2018 and 2022.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses legal recognition of gender markers on passports or identity documents, entry or visa screening that could disclose a traveller's gender history, access to healthcare including HIV-related care, or facility and restroom rules. These remain unsourced for South Sudan.

The inventory does not establish whether the cross-dressing provision has been enforced at any point. The State Department non-enforcement finding attaches to the same-sex conduct provision; whether the dress provision has produced prosecutions is unresolved on these sources.

The three-month penalty for the cross-dressing offence is drawn from secondary country coverage rather than the Penal Code text, and is not corroborated by the State Department reports, which state the provision without giving a penalty.

Reported non-enforcement is not decriminalisation. No source indicates repeal, a moratorium or a stated prosecutorial policy, and non-enforcement recorded by one government's annual reporting cannot be read as a legal change.

The sourced coverage ends with the 2022 reporting year. No material in the inventory establishes the state of enforcement, official rhetoric or the security environment in later years, and no hate-crime or violence statistics are available.
